mission: Use the documented 1901 discovery, modern loss, surviving textile/photographic/jewellery proxies, and independently dated human material from Djer Tomb O to test how real human biological material intersects a monument later treated as the Tomb of Osiris, without identifying any human remain as Osiris.

core_finding.site: Abydos, Umm el-Qa'ab, Tomb O of King Djer
core_finding.later_reception: In the Middle Kingdom and later the tomb was considered the burial place/tomb of Osiris.
core_finding.1901_discovery: Petrie's team recovered a linen-wrapped human forearm hidden in a wall hole/niche with four bracelets still in place.
core_finding.primary_excavator_interpretation: Petrie described the jewellery as belonging to Djer's queen and reconstructed the arm as part of a plundered royal female body.
core_finding.modern_identity_dispute: The Global Egyptian Museum describes the forearm as female, possibly Djer's queen or royal-family member; later scholarship has also argued it may have been Djer himself. Identity therefore remains unresolved.
core_finding.modern_loss: After transfer to the Cairo Museum, the arm itself was discarded; the bracelets were retained as JE 35054.
core_finding.importance: This is a literal lost human body member from a tomb that ancient Egyptians later treated as the Tomb of Osiris. It is not evidence that the arm belonged to Osiris; it is an unusually strong biological-and-cult-context control for the missing-member search.

surviving_proxies.description: Photograph of the linen-wrapped/unwrapped arm with bracelets; EES identifies the image as AB-RT.NEG.II.005.
Four bracelets recovered in situ on the forearm; physical ordering was documented before removal.

Three dark-brown friable linen fragments from Djer's royal tomb; UCL explicitly cites Petrie 1901 p.16 and the discovery of the arm with linen wrappings. EES states small fragments of resin-soaked linen bandages from the arm survive as UC35716.

tomb_o_human_material_controls.database_model_coordinate: approximately 3095 BCE in the cited IntChron series; use calibrated/model publication for formal chronological interpretation
tomb_o_human_material_controls.published_data: Dee et al. 2012/2013 Early Egypt chronology datasets
tomb_o_human_material_controls.importance: A Tomb O human-hair sample independently returns an Early Dynastic radiocarbon result, correcting older uncertainty that all surviving Djer-tomb hair might be later Osirian votive material.
tomb_o_human_material_controls.firewall: The hair is not documented as coming from the lost bracelet-bearing arm and must not be treated as tissue from that individual.

tomb_o_human_material_controls.description: Human hair/plaits/false fringe attributed to Djer Tomb O; museum human-remains list identifies 1901.40.52-55 as Tomb of Djer material.
tomb_o_human_material_controls.chronology_caution: Object-level context within the tomb is imperfect; only tested samples should receive radiocarbon status individually.

critical_correction.older_problem: Earlier scholarship warned that large quantities of hair from Tomb O might be New Kingdom/later Osirian cult deposits and that provenance was imperfect.
critical_correction.new_control: OxA-23195 on PRM 1901.40.53 is a human-hair radiocarbon measurement in the Early Dynastic range, and IntChron explicitly associates the sample with Djer, Tomb O.
critical_correction.consequence: The surviving Tomb O biological corpus is heterogeneous in contextual certainty but cannot be dismissed wholesale as later cult material. Individual samples require object-level dating and context tests.

next_actions: Request EES archive metadata/high-resolution image for AB-RT.NEG.II.005 plus any excavation diary, distribution, correspondence or Cairo-transfer documentation for the arm.
Request UCL Petrie Museum conservation/analysis history for UC35716/UC35716a, including whether resin chemistry, microscopy or adhering biological residues have ever been assessed.

Request Egyptian Museum registration/history for JE35054 and any surviving accession, disposal, correspondence or old-register note concerning the forearm and wrappings transferred with the bracelets.

Request Pitt Rivers object-level documentation and analysis history for 1901.40.52-56, especially OxA-23195 sample selection, remaining material, precise internal context and whether other samples have been dated or biomolecularly characterized.
Keep all human-remains work non-destructive by default; any destructive analysis requires institutional ethics, legal and conservation approval.
Compare Tomb O biological dates with the later Osiris-cult phases of the monument to distinguish Early Dynastic royal/retainer material from later devotional deposits.

relation_to_missing_parts_hunt.reason: Unlike most Osiris-member traditions, this branch contains a documented real human member, a later Osiris-tomb identity for the monument, a modern loss event, and surviving physical/photographic proxies capable of further testing.
relation_to_missing_parts_hunt.decision_use: If surviving proxies confirm only Early Dynastic royal context, the branch demonstrates later Osirian reinterpretation of older human remains. If any independently dated biological material securely belongs to later cult deposition, it would demonstrate human biological material entering an Osiris sanctuary in a later phase, still without identifying it as Osiris.

canonical_formula: LATER_OSIRIS_TOMB_IDENTITY + REAL_HUMAN_MEMBER + MODERN_LOSS + SURVIVING_PROXY + INDEPENDENT_C14_CONTROLS => HIGH_VALUE_BIOLOGICAL_CONTROL; NOT OSIRIS_IDENTITY
canonical_seal: A REAL ARM WAS FOUND IN A TOMB LATER WORSHIPPED AS OSIRIS'S TOMB, AND MODERN HANDS LOST IT. FOLLOW THE SURVIVING LINEN, PHOTOGRAPH, JEWELLERY AND DATED HUMAN MATERIAL—BUT NEVER TURN THE TOMB'S DIVINE NAME INTO THE PERSON'S IDENTITY.
